en.a11yBox: Empty box. Drop a name here.
en.a11yChip: {name}. Drag it to a box, or press to pick it up.
en.a11ySlider: Angle slider. Use the arrow keys to move it.
en.s1Hello: Let’s explore how a triangle helps us find trigonometric values.
en.s1Here: Here’s a right-angled triangle. We’ll call this angle theta.
en.s1Recall: Before we begin, let’s recall the side names for this angle.
en.s1Match: Can you match each side to its name?
en.s1MatchDone: That’s correct! These are the opposite side, adjacent side and hypotenuse.
en.s1Other: What if we look at the triangle from this angle instead?
en.s1Swap: The opposite and adjacent swap roles. The hypotenuse stays the same.
en.s2Back: Let’s go back to our first angle and recall the ratios.
en.s2SinAsk: Which two sides make up sin theta? Choose them here.
en.s2CosAsk: How about cos theta? Choose the two sides.
en.s2TanAsk: And which two sides do we use for tan theta?
en.s2UseRatios: Now let’s use these ratios to find the values for a few familiar angles.
en.s2Slide45: Move the slider to 45°. Watch what happens to the triangle.
en.s2Now45: There we go! The angle is now 45°.
en.s2Missing: We know two angles. Can you find the missing one?
en.s2Both45: Both angles are 45°, so the sides opposite them are equal too.
en.s2Base1: Let’s choose a base of 1 unit. The other equal side is also 1 unit.
en.s2PythHyp: Can you use Pythagoras’ theorem to find the hypotenuse?
en.s2AllThree: Now we have all three lengths.
en.s2Sin45: Let’s use these lengths to find sin 45°.
en.s2YourTurn45: Your turn! Use this triangle to find cos 45° and tan 45°.
en.s2Found45: We’ve found all three values for 45°.
en.s2AddTable: Let’s add them to our table.
en.s2Next3060: Next up are 30° and 60°. One triangle will help us find both!
en.s3Equi: This time, let’s start with an equilateral triangle.
en.s3AllEqual: All three sides are equal, and every angle is 60°.
en.s3Len2: Let’s choose a length of 2 units for each side.
en.s3TapSplit: Tap here to split the triangle into two matching halves.
en.s3Perp: The perpendicular halves the base and the 60° angle.
en.s3EachHalf: Each half is a right-angled triangle.
en.s3KeepOne: We only need one half. Let’s keep this one.
en.s3PythB: Can you use Pythagoras’ theorem to find b?
en.s3Root3: That gives us √3 units. Now we have all three lengths.
en.s3Sin30: Let’s use them to find sin 30°.
en.s3YourTurn30: Now you try. What are cos 30° and tan 30°?
en.s3AddTable: Let’s add the 30° values to our table.
en.s3Leaves60: That leaves 60°. Can we use the triangle we already have?
en.s3Yes60: Yes! The other acute angle in this triangle is 60°.
en.s4Use60: Let’s use 60° as our reference angle this time.
en.s4Roles: Now √3 is opposite and 1 is adjacent. The hypotenuse is still 2.
en.s4YourTurn60: Use the same lengths to find cos 60° and tan 60°.
en.s4AddTable: Let’s add these to our table too.
en.s5Closer0: What happens as the angle gets closer to 0°?
en.s5Slide0: Move the slider and watch the sides.
en.s5At0: At 0°, the opposite side becomes zero. The other two sides overlap.
en.s5Extend0: Let’s use these distances to extend the ratios to 0°.
en.s5AddTable: Let’s add the 0° values to our table.
en.s6Explore90: Now let’s explore 90°. Move the slider and watch A move towards B.
en.s6Closer: As A gets closer to B, AB gets shorter and AC gets closer to 4.
en.s6At90: At 90°, A reaches B, so the adjacent side becomes zero. The other two sides overlap.
en.s6Line: Again, we have a line. Let’s use these distances to extend the ratios to 90°.
en.s6Undefined: We can’t divide by zero, so tan 90° is undefined.
en.s7Complete: Our table is complete! You’ve found the sine, cosine and tangent values for all five angles.
